reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: A monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease in which non-organised, non-amyloid monoclonal light chains (most often kappa) deposit along basement membranes
Presents commonly with proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, hypertension and progressive renal impairment, frequently with nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy
Deposits are Congo-red negative and lack the fibrillar or microtubular organisation of amyloid and immunotactoid disease
Immunofluorescence shows monoclonal light-chain restriction along glomerular and tubular basement membranes; electron microscopy shows granular, punctate electron-dense deposits
Reflects an underlying plasma-cell or B-cell clone, so a monoclonal gammopathy workup is mandatory, and it may accompany myeloma
It falls within the spectrum of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance when the clone is small but nephrotoxic
Treatment is clone-directed therapy for the paraprotein-related disease alongside renin-angiotensin blockade and supportive care
reference.pathophysiology: Light chain deposition disease arises from a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell population that secretes a monoclonal light chain with physicochemical properties favouring tissue deposition rather than fibril formation. The light chains deposit as granular, non-Congophilic material along the glomerular and tubular basement membranes and in the mesangium, where they stimulate mesangial matrix production and nodular expansion resembling diabetic glomerulosclerosis. Tubular basement membrane deposition contributes to tubulointerstitial injury. The result is progressive proteinuria, nodular glomerulosclerosis and declining renal function; because the causative clone may be small, the systemic tumour burden can be modest even when renal damage is substantial.
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence showing monoclonal light-chain restriction and electron microscopy showing granular deposits
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation
Serum free light chains and the free light-chain ratio
Bone marrow examination for a plasma-cell clone and to assess for myeloma
Skeletal survey or cross-sectional imaging and calcium where myeloma is suspected
redFlags: Features of overt multiple myeloma such as hypercalcaemia, anaemia or bone lesions
Coexisting cardiac or hepatic light-chain deposition
reference.prognosis: Renal and overall outcome depend on the underlying clone and its response to clone-directed therapy; suppression of the pathogenic light chain can stabilise or improve renal function, whereas advanced renal impairment at diagnosis and coexisting myeloma predict worse outcomes. Extra-renal deposition, particularly cardiac, further worsens prognosis, and the disease may recur after transplantation if the clone is not controlled.
pitfalls: Mistaking nodular glomerulosclerosis for diabetic nephropathy without immunofluorescence
Confusing it with amyloidosis when Congo-red staining is not performed
Failing to identify and treat the underlying clone
Overlooking small but nephrotoxic clones within the monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance spectrum
Not screening for concurrent cast nephropathy and myeloma
management: Give clone-directed treatment tailored to the underlying plasma-cell or B-cell clone, commonly bortezomib-based (proteasome inhibitor) regimens with corticosteroids and autologous stem-cell transplantation where appropriate, even when the clone is small in monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance
Treat coexisting multiple myeloma when present
Apply renoprotective measures with renin-angiotensin blockade and blood-pressure control, plus management of nephrotic syndrome
Monitor serum free light-chain levels and ratio as the key marker of treatment response, alongside renal function
Assess for extrarenal deposition and treat accordingly
Use renal replacement therapy for end-stage disease, deferring transplantation until the clone is in sustained remission
Manage jointly between nephrology and haematology given the disorder's monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance
